Icon wells, quieter

Three treatments, one real icon set, and the numbers that say which is calmest
REVISED  sheet 02 §03 · every row in the app
ICONS    Lucide · ISC · real paths
HEXES    unchanged — §D3 still locked
DATE     2026-07-30

You're right, and it's two problems stacked

A solid 40×40 block at full domain saturation is the heaviest object on the row — heavier than the amount, heavier than the title. It out-shouts the thing it's supposed to be labelling.

Emoji then makes it worse: each one drags in its own palette — a red-and-white fuel pump, a blue wrench — so the row shows two colour systems fighting inside one 40px square. Emoji also renders differently per platform, which quietly breaks "worn identically" on the Android half of the project.

What stays fixed

The four hexes are §D3 law and none of them changes here. What changes is how much area each hue is asked to cover — which is a design decision the spec leaves entirely open.

All three options below still answer "what kind of money is this" with hue, still wear it identically across wells, chart series and detail chrome, and still keep semantic colours out of the set.

Why Lucide

ISC-licensed, ~1.600 glyphs, drawn on one 24px grid with a single stroke weight — so every icon in the app is guaranteed to share a voice, including the ones nobody has specified yet.

These are the real paths, pulled from the repo, set at stroke 1.75 rather than the shipped 2 — at 20px the default reads slightly chunky against Koi's type.

Three ways down

Same icons, same hexes, three amounts of colour. 1a is my recommendation.

Each is shown as the eight-glyph set, then in a real row stack, light and dark. Read them at a distance first — the question is which column still tells you what kind of money each row is, while looking like paper rather than a legend.

1a Tinted well RECOMMENDED

The well keeps its shape and its hue, but as a wash; the icon carries the saturated step. Colour area drops by roughly nine tenths — the hue is still unmistakably there, it just stops being the loudest thing on the row.

Why this one

It is already the app's language. The status chips on sheet 02 are exactly this — #F3E9F1 wash, #6E3960 label. Adopting it for wells means one treatment covers chips and wells both, instead of two ideas about what a hue looks like at rest.

The cost

Wells stop being scannable from a metre away. That is a real loss and I think a correct trade — nobody scans a ledger from a metre away, and the row title is the faster read anyway.

1b No well at all

Drop the container. The icon sits directly on the paper in its domain hue, at 22px. This is the quietest the row can get while still being colour-coded at all — and the most like a printed ledger.

What it wins

The calmest of the three by a clear margin, and the icons get to be drawings rather than marks squeezed into a box. Fewest tokens too — no wash set to maintain.

Why I stopped short of it

Two real costs. The column stops reading as a column — glyph silhouettes differ enough that the left edge gets ragged. And a bare hue at 22px is a thin target for the fuel/service pair to be told apart by, where 1a's wash gives the eye a second, larger cue.

1c Ring

The container survives as a 1px hue ring on the card surface, with the icon in the same saturated step. Keeps the column dead straight; spends almost no colour area doing it.

What it wins

The straightest column of the three, and the crispest at small sizes — a 1px ring survives where a wash can get lost on a bright screen outdoors.

Where it strains

Outlined boxes read as interactive — they look like the option chips and the input fields, which are tappable. And a full-saturation hairline is surprisingly insistent: this is quieter than the baseline but noticeably busier than 1a.

The numbers behind the recommendation

Block weight — the well against the paper. Lower is calmer. Icon legibility — the glyph against its own well. Needs ≥3:1.

The inversion is the whole argument

Today the well shouts at the page (4:1 against paper) and whispers at its own icon. 1a swaps that: the block drops to roughly 1,1:1 against the paper — nearly invisible as a shape — while the icon climbs above the current figure. More legible, far quieter. That is not a compromise, it is the correct assignment of contrast.

Considered and rejected: muted hues

The obvious fix is to desaturate the four hues themselves. It fails §D3 — the hue a bar wears and the hue a well wears must be the same hue, so muting the well means muting the whole chart grammar, or keeping two versions of every domain colour. Tinting the surface while the hue itself stays locked gets the same calm with no second palette.

Five new tokens either way

Two of the light washes already exist in the build as chip backgrounds. 1a formalises them as a domainWash ramp — four hues plus ink, light and dark — so chips and wells stop being separately invented.
